item.title: Students’ intention to engage with hypothetical AI-recommended ESG campaigns: Integrating TPB and UTAUT via perceived AI competence and trust in AI
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
As digital platforms increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to curate content, university students may encounter environmental, social, and governance (ESG) campaigns through algorithmic recommendation systems. This study examined students’ perceptions and stated intention to engage with AI-recommended ESG campaigns within a standardized hypothetical scenario. Participants were not exposed to an operational AI recommendation system, and actual ESG participation was not measured. The study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with selected UTAUT antecedents and two AI-specific constructs: perceived AI competence and trust in AI. Survey data were collected from undergraduate students at one Vietnamese university (N = 218), with 199 valid responses retained after screening and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with perceived AI competence, which was positively associated with trust in AI. Trust in AI was positively associated with attitude, while attitude showed the largest standardized association with engagement intention. Perceived behavioral control was also positively associated with intention, whereas subjective norm was not significant. Bootstrapped indirect effects were consistent with sequential associations linking technology-related beliefs to intention through perceived AI competence, trust in AI, and attitude. Academic year positively moderated the performance expectancy–competence association (β = 0.112, p = .027), such that this association was stronger in higher academic years; the effort expectancy–competence interaction was not statistically significant. These findings concern perceptions and stated behavioral intentions within a hypothetical scenario and should not be interpreted as evidence of actual AI exposure or ESG participation.

item.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

item.title: Generative AI feedback use and English writing self-regulation among Chinese non-English majors: a two-wave study of feedback literacy and writing anxiety
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Methods Non-English-major undergraduates at three universities in Henan Province, China, completed two surveys 12 weeks apart in the 2026 spring semester (wave 1 N = 650; 520 retained, 80.0%). Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. The generative AI feedback use scale is a preliminary study-specific measure.

item.title: Making learning visible in the age of generative AI: reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

item.title: Latent profile analysis of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates: associations with positive acceptance and striving
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

item.title: Interpersonal academic help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency: the roles of stigma, shame, and perceived anonymity
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has emerged as a new source of academic support for university students. However, students' willingness to seek academic help may also be influenced by social evaluation concerns surrounding traditional interpersonal help-seeking. This study examines how academic help-seeking (AHS) stigma relates to interpersonal help-seeking avoidance through academic shame, and whether interpersonal avoidance is associated with GAI help-seeking tendency under different levels of perceived anonymity. Methods Two independent cross-sectional survey studies were conducted among Chinese university students. Study 1 examined the relationships among AHS stigma, academic shame, and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance using data from 183 undergraduate students. Study 2 extended the model with a sample of 401 university students by examining the relationship between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency, as well as the moderating role of perceived anonymity. PLS-SEM was used to test the proposed relationships. Results Across both studies, AHS stigma was positively associated with interpersonal help-seeking avoidance. Academic shame showed significant indirect associations between AHS stigma and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance in both studies. Study 2 further showed that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance was positively associated with GAI help-seeking tendency. Moreover, perceived anonymity positively moderated this relationship, such that the positive association between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency was stronger at higher levels of perceived anonymity. Discussion The findings highlight the social-emotional dimensions of academic help-seeking, showing that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance can coexist with a greater willingness to seek support from GAI tools. Perceived anonymity further conditions this association, suggesting that the perceived social visibility of help-seeking is relevant to students' support preferences. These findings extend the understanding of GAI-assisted academic help-seeking beyond technology-related considerations, while distinguishing help-seeking tendencies from actual changes in support-source use.

item.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students: a cross-sectional study across educational levels
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective To examine educational-level differences in artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students, and the independent associations of AI anxiety with the two academic outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 1,168 music students from 14 Chinese universities across eight provinces and municipalities (824 undergraduates, 276 master’s students, and 68 doctoral students). Welch’s ANOVA, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), adjusted general linear models, and hierarchical multiple regression were used to examine group differences and associations. AI anxiety × educational-level interactions were also tested. Results Adjusted educational-level effects were small (partial η 2 = 0.017 for AI anxiety, 0.011 for academic engagement, and 0.012 for academic burnout; multivariate partial η 2 = 0.008 for engagement and burnout jointly). Adjusted comparisons showed differences among all three educational levels in AI anxiety. Undergraduates reported lower academic engagement than both postgraduate groups. For burnout, undergraduates scored higher than master’s students, while the undergraduate–doctoral difference was not significant. AI anxiety correlated negatively with academic engagement ( r = −0.166) and positively with academic burnout ( r = 0.361). After adjustment, AI anxiety remained negatively associated with engagement ( β = −0.141) and positively associated with burnout ( β = 0.332). Neither association varied significantly across educational levels. Conclusion Educational-level differences in AI anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout were small. AI anxiety was independently associated with both academic outcomes, with no significant moderation by educational level. These findings highlight the importance of considering students’ psychological experiences when integrating AI into higher music education.

item.title: An interpretable machine learning framework for student depression risk prediction: integrating multi-domain features with SHAP-based explainability
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Depression among university students constitutes a pressing global mental health challenge, with prevalence rates exceeding 30% in numerous populations. While traditional screening instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) offer effective clinical detection, they are inherently reactive and focus solely on symptom assessment, lacking the ability to capture modifiable risk factors. Machine learning (ML) approaches, particularly ensemble methods with explainability frameworks, present a promising avenue for risk stratification using multi-domain data. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable XGBoost-based prediction model integrating academic, demographic, lifestyle, and clinical features to predict student depression risk, and to systematically evaluate model performance, feature contributions, and clinical utility using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and Decision Curve Analysis (DCA). Methods A cross-sectional dataset of 27,901 student records with 16 multi-domain features was analyzed. XGBoost was trained with 80/20 stratified split (n_train = 22,320, n_test = 5,581). Model performance was assessed via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration (Brier score), and DCA. Feature importance was quantified through SHAP values, and eight predefined hypotheses concerning risk factor directionality, dose-response relationships, and domain contributions were tested. Results The XGBoost model achieved AUC = 0.919, accuracy = 0.845, F1-score = 0.869, and Brier score = 0.111. The strongest predictors by mean | SHAP| were suicidal ideation (1.212), Academic Pressure (0.934), and Financial Stress (0.679). Financial Stress and Work/Study Hours demonstrated clear monotonic dose-response relationships. CGPA showed significant linear association (R 2 = 0.473, p < 0.001). The multi-domain model significantly outperformed all single-domain models ( p < 0.001). DCA confirmed net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities of 10%–50%. A sensitivity model excluding suicidal ideation maintained good performance (AUC = 0.868), supporting its practical utility in ethically constrained screening contexts. Conclusion The XGBoost + SHAP framework demonstrates robust predictive performance, excellent calibration, and clinically meaningful interpretability for student depression risk assessment. Multi-domain integration is essential for comprehensive risk profiling. These findings support the development of explainable ML-based screening tools for educational mental health settings.

item.title: AI usage, large language model dependence, and critical thinking among university students: the mediating roles of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

item.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

item.title: When GenAI helps and when it hurts: testing expertise reversal within a cognitive load framework across different guidance, task complexity, and GenAI access conditions
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract Studies have examined the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on students’ learning outcomes, revealing a wide range of effects on performance, cognitive load, and learning processes. However, little is known about whether these effects change with learner expertise and the conditions under which GenAI support is provided. This study examined expertise reversal in GenAI-supported programming education across four eight-week experiments involving Year 3 computer science students from research universities in Saudi Arabia. Drawing on cognitive load theory, the experiments investigated GenAI support, guidance level, task complexity, and access condition in relation to intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, mental effort, and independent programming performance. The findings showed that GenAI support produced greater reductions in extraneous load and stronger independent performance among lower-expertise learners, while higher-expertise learners retained smaller benefits. Detailed guidance produced a crossover expertise reversal, benefiting lower-expertise learners while increasing extraneous load and weakening performance among higher-expertise learners. Higher task complexity increased cognitive demands and reduced performance across expertise levels, with greater effects among lower-expertise learners. Personalised access also benefited lower-expertise learners more strongly without disadvantaging higher-expertise learners. Overall, the findings distinguish a crossover expertise reversal under detailed GenAI guidance from diminishing benefits as learner expertise increases under other support and access conditions. The effects of task complexity further demonstrate that expertise-dependent differences do not necessarily constitute a reversal in instructional effectiveness. We recommend that effective GenAI support requires careful calibration to learners’ existing knowledge and the cognitive demands of learning.
